scope: MEAS: Internet Archive metadata and file listing for bp-2-berg-suite-lyrique-iv, MD5 of the cached MP3 against the manifest, loudness traces at 0.25–0.5 s, tuning estimate, the label photograph BP2 label 3.JPG (viewed); EXT: The American Music Lover, vol. 2 no. 11, March 1937 (OCR text and advertisement, printed pp. 377 and 385), Wikipedia (Lyric Suite, Berg), Steinberg’s note on bso.org, Jarman (Musicologica Austriaca, 2017), the Interlude article on the Galimir Quartet. Not an aural review.

corrections.finding: The return of the Allegro misterioso stood at 149 s. The Trio estatico ends on its climax at about 148.5 s (the loudest point of the file is at 2:25), and the level falls from about −19 dB to −38 dB between 150 and 154 s, so the quiet reprise is under way by about 151.5 s. The Trio’s own start at 93.7 s (a step from −31 dB to −22 dB) agrees with the 94 s boundary.
corrections.fix: Section A′ and the return cue moved to 150 s; bases of the Trio and return cues changed to audio-feature.

corrections.finding: The intro called the movement “a scherzo in three parts”. None of the cited sources uses the word; Wikipedia gives an ABA form.
corrections.fix: Intro now says the movement has a Trio estatico between two statements of the Allegro misterioso.

corrections.finding: The 1937 advertisement lists, besides sets BP No. 1–3, Nos. 4 and 6 (Beethoven’s Op. 106, Bach’s English Suite No. 3) and disc 95034 (Milhaud). The return note rested on Wikipedia alone although Jarman states the retrograde relation and quotes Berg’s annotation “Vergessen Sie es” at its start.
corrections.fix: The American-issue evidence says “among others”; Jarman added to the return note’s evidence.

corrections.finding: The dossier did not use the label photograph in the Archive item, which names the disc (95007), the part (Part III of 8), the set (BP-2) and “Recorded in France”, and it did not record that Wikipedia lists different French catalogue numbers (Polydor 595.135–595.138 against the item’s 516.659–516.662) and the date “ca. 1935”.
corrections.fix: Label added as source; matrixTakeSides, catalogue, session place and date fields updated; the unreconciled numbers are stated as such.

checks.source: The Archive lists BP2 Berg Suite Lyrique (iii).mp3 as a derivative VBR MP3, 222.09 s, beside the FLAC original; the cached copy has the manifest MD5 (8a73f615…). The sound starts at 0.3 s and ends at 217.6 s, followed by 4.4 s of digital silence. No licence field in the metadata.
checks.durationAndPitch: 3:42, one side of the set: the label of disc 95007 reads “In 8 Parts, Part III, Set No. BP-2 … Third Movement: Allegro misterioso”. INFERENCE: six movements on eight parts fit the six Archive files if the longer movements IV and VI take two parts each. Tuning estimate −5 cents (windows −1 to −15 cents), A about 439 Hz; no transposition or speed correction needed.
checks.identity: Label (viewed): Brunswick Polydor 95007, “Suite Lyrique (For String Quartet), Third Movement: Allegro misterioso (Alban Berg), Galimir String Quartet of Vienna”, “Made in U.S.A.”, “Recorded in France”, label copy 1937. Archive description: Felix, Adrielle [sic], Renée and Marguerite Galimir, recorded c. 1935–36 in Paris for French Polydor, Brunswick-Polydor BP-2 in March 1937. BSO note: the quartet consisted of a brother and three sisters, the second violinist Adrienne Galimir. Wikipedia: Galimir Quartet, ca. 1935. The Archive’s Polydor and Decca numbers and the December 1936 British date were not confirmed elsewhere.
checks.notes: Wikipedia supports the A–B–H–F motif, its prominence in the third movement, the dedication to Zemlinsky, the ABA form with a through-composed Trio and the forwards-then-backwards outer sections; Steinberg’s note supports Perle and Green, the Fuchs-Robettin affair and Krasner’s meeting with the Galimirs; Jarman supports the retrograde. The March 1937 magazine supports the last note. Times: A 0 s, Trio 94 s, return 150 s fit the loudness profile, with the Trio the loudest and most active stretch (1:35 to 2:27). Counts: 6 notes, limit 6. Voice rules read by hand and by the validator; validate.mjs prints ok for the listen file and the dossier.
checks.sideJoins: The movement occupies a single side (Part III); no join falls inside it.

rights.decision: Publish on the territorial basis stated in the file.
rights.reasoning: (1) First publication: The American Music Lover, March 1937, printed p. 385, carries a Brunswick-Polydor advertisement listing “Set BP No. 2. ALBAN BERG: Suite Lyrique. For String Quartet. Galimir String Quartet of Vienna”; the magazine’s review pages (p. 377) say the new recordings “were placed on the market just before we went to press” and call Berg’s Lyric Suite provocative; the label carries a 1937 copyright line. The Archive description gives earlier issues in France and Britain (Decca, December 1936), which would only advance the date and were not verified. A recording published in 1937 had no 50-year EU term left after 1987. (2) Provenance: a commercial issue (“Recorded in France”, an American re-pressing of French Polydor), not a live or broadcast capture, and not a modern re-labelling. (3) Composition: Berg died in 1935, public domain in the EU since 2006; the dossier states the United States status is not assessed. (4) The United States status of a recording made in France in the 1930s is not established and the dossier says so.
rights.internetArchiveFlags: No licence field; collections shellackophile-recordings, 78rpm, audio_music; no dark, access-restricted, noindex or litigation flag; uploaded as FLAC with MP3 derivative.

observations.finding: The Archive description gives Polydor 516.659–516.662 for the French issue; Wikipedia’s list of recordings gives Polydor 595.135–595.138. Both are recorded in the dossier as unreconciled.
observations.action: No change to the work or the cues; a catalogue of the French Polydor series would settle it.
